item.text: {"schema":"voice-critic-source/1","findings":[{"location":"Line 5: “Approval should require a written data processing agreement (DPA), a clear statement that submitted content won’t train models, defined retention and deletion periods, encryption, access controls such as multifactor authentication (MFA), breach notification, and a list of subprocessors.”","what":"This shifts into an enterprise compliance-checklist register that is more procedural and institutionally technical than the corpus’s public-facing advocacy voice.","corpus_evidence":"Across all eleven samples, technical requirements are explained through concrete consequences for ordinary users rather than presented as procurement controls; for example, “why-are-gay-bars-building-databases-their-patrons.txt” says, “Personal data is routinely stolen by thieves, misused by a company’s employees, seized by government agencies, and diverted to new purposes by a company’s executives.”","confidence":"high"},{"location":"Lines 5–7: “If those answers can’t be obtained in writing, stop. For the meeting, propose a narrow pilot using invented or fully synthetic notes … Assign one staff owner to review every output and prohibit automatic entry into client records.”","what":"The sustained sequence of operational directives sounds like an internal implementation memo, unlike the corpus’s pattern of arguing for a policy conclusion through stated harms and consequences.","corpus_evidence":"The corpus does use occasional calls to action, but not sustained workplace procedure; “congress-narrowed-guard-act-serious-problems-remain.txt,” for example, moves from consequence to conclusion: “Smaller developers, in particular, may decide it is safer to block younger users entirely … rather than risk severe penalties under vague standards.”","confidence":"high"}],"clean_categories":["unfamiliar-constructions","unvarying-voice"],"rhythm_assessed":false,"rhythm_note":"Category 4 was not assessed because no deterministic rhythm scan was supplied.","verdict":"REVISE"}
